newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: FEATURE - Political instability may undermine Macedonia recovery.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Political instability may undermine Macedonia recovery.

text.p: Macedonia's ethnic tensions and high unemployment, coupled with political instability in the Balkans, may endanger this former Yugoslav republic's assertive economic reform performance and optimistic prospects for growth.

"I believe we are at a critical turning point where the public could begin to see the positive effects of the reforms...but unfortunately political instability may undermine the economic performance that we envisioned for the next few years," said Ellen Goldstein, the World Bank's resident representative in Skopje.
Living standards have fallen sharply in the six years since this landlocked republic declared independence from Yugoslavia.
Although Macedonia was not drawn into war, its economy, heavily integrated with the rest of Yugoslavia, was badly hit by the break-up of the country.
The United Nations sanctions on neighbouring Serbia and a crippling trade blockade by Greece, which ended in October 1995, have also taken a heavy toll.
"Macedonia has performed admirably in stabilising the economy...in a troubled region, in a period of time in which a country was suffering many exogenous impacts," Goldstein told Reuters.

Annual inflation dropped sharply from 2,000 percent in 1993 to three percent last year as a result of a tough restrictive policy backed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. The budget deficit fell from 13 percent to less than one percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The government envisages five percent average annual GDP growth for this and the next three years. Macedonia's current targets are economic recovery, creation of jobs and encouraging private sector growth, said the World Bank.
COST OF MACROECONOMIC STABILITY SEEN AS UNJUSTIFIED
However local economists say the cost of macroeconomic stability resulting in a stagnant industry and a high unemployment, was unjustifiably high.
Unemployment, according to different estimates, ranges between 25 percent and 35 percent of a 620,000 work force.
Industrial output grew by 3.2 percent in 1996, but fell by 15 percent in February and 10 percent in December. The country posted a $600 million trade deficit last year.

With 90 percent of the economy privatised, mostly through management buy-outs, cash-starved industry has yet to seek strategic investors that would bring in fresh capital, new management skills and technology.
Ten percent of industry, which includes the Skopje metalworks and other big state-owned loss-making factories, has yet to be restructured and privatised.

"Unless the government boosts investment in production at the risk of slightly fuelling inflation, living standards will continue falling and the number of jobless will increase," said Boris Stojmenov, owner of financial consultancy firm BS Holding.
"In several months people may take to the streets like they did in Bulgaria," he told Reuters.
NATIONALIST TENSIONS GROWING
Nationalist tensions are growing in Macedonia as its ethnic Albanians demand more autonomy while Macedonian students protest against the use of Albanian in educational programmes.
"When you combine highly politicised issues with an unemployment rate of such a level, you have a recipe for multiple explosiveness," said Goldstein.
Diplomats say the opposition may also use Albanian nationalist sentiments in a call for early elections.
Ethnic Albanians officially account for 22 percent of Macedonia's population of almost two million.

"Macedonia has made remarkable efforts to be a peaceful multi-ethnic society. They have moved forward on reform overcoming major exogenous economic obstacles...It will be a tragedy to disrupt all this," said Goldstein.
